reading.body:
The single most useful fact here is negative: a record tagged as a data center carries a name that gives no sign of any computing business, and its status is unconfirmed.

The record is an OpenStreetMap node in Spain, tagged telecom=data_center, named The Weaver. The name points toward textiles, craft, or a hospitality or creative business rather than IT or hosting. The research note states plainly that the tag may have been misapplied to an unrelated premises, and that this could not be confirmed because the search quota was exhausted. No operator, no website, and no megawatt figure are recorded.

For AI infrastructure this matters as a data-quality signal rather than a capacity one. Every serious estimate of data-center buildout, and therefore of the power and buildings behind compute, ultimately rests on facility inventories. If a share of those inventories is mislabeled, the error runs in both directions: phantom facilities inflate counts, and the same tagging weakness can hide real ones. A single unverified node is not evidence of a trend, but it is a concrete example of how the underlying lists are assembled and where they can fail.

What the data does not tell the reader is whether a data center exists at this location at all. It records no capacity, no operator, and no confirmation either way. The one physical detail is proximity: the site is 1.9 miles from Alicante-Elche Miguel Hernández Airport. That is a location fact, not a finding about compute, power, or the grid, and it should not be read as one.
